body.statement:
For \(n_B=n_S=n\), one has \(\Phi_{n,n}(R)\ge \Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(R)\) for every \(R\). In particular, for \(R=4\) and every \(n\ge3\),
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)=2(n-1)^2+2,
\qquad
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\le n^2,
\]
and equality in the second display holds if and only if \(n\) is even. Consequently,
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\ge (n-2)^2>0
\]
and
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
\ge 2-\frac4n+\frac4{n^2}.
\]
Equality in the ratio bound holds if and only if \(n\) is even. Thus this lower bound tends to \(2\), the actual ratio tends to \(2\) along the even integers, and its limit inferior over all integers \(n\to\infty\) equals \(2\).
body.justification: An infinite exact separation shows that the catalog is not merely a notational enlargement of the published equal-block family: at every balanced square with support four, unequal blocks strictly improve focal retention, with a sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope.
body.gap: The published equal-square calculation optimizes only over equal block sizes and therefore misses the exact unequal-block optimum even on every balanced square at support four.
body.consumer: Researchers using the published equal-block rule obtain a certified focal-size improvement for every balanced population size at least three, without changing the underlying independent balanced randomization.
body.proof_tex:
First fix \(n_B=n_S=n\) and an arbitrary \(R\). For each positive divisor \(k\mid n\), form the equal-square profile with
\[
L=\frac{2n}{k},\qquad a_\ell=b_\ell=k\quad(\ell\in[L]).
\]
The two covering sums are
\[
\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}a_\ell=Lk=2n,
\qquad
\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}b_\ell=Lk=2n.
\]
By the definition of common support, a vector \(z\in\{0,1\}^{L}\) belongs to \(H(a,b)\) exactly when
\[
k\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}z_\ell=n,
\]
the buyer and seller equations being identical. Since \(k\mid n\), this is equivalent to \(\sum_\ell z_\ell=n/k\), and therefore
\[
h(a,b)=\binom{2n/k}{n/k}.
\]
The retention definition gives
\[
F(a,b)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}k^2=Lk^2=2nk.
\]
Hence every divisor appearing in the maximum defining \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(R)\) produces a member of \(\mathcal A_{n,n}(R)\) having the same objective value. Maximizing first over that equal-square subfamily and then over the full admissible class proves
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(R)\ge \Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(R).
\]
If the comparator's defining set is empty, its value is \(-\infty\) by definition and the same inequality holds in the extended order.

Now take \(R=4\) and \(n\ge3\). Proposition \texttt{prop:r4-reduction} applies and yields
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)=2(n-1)(n-1)+2=2(n-1)^2+2.
\]
For the equal-square comparator, \(k=n\) has
\[
h(a,b)=\binom21=2<4,
\]
so it is infeasible. Every eligible divisor is consequently a proper divisor of \(n\). If \(k\) is a proper positive divisor, then \(n/k\) is an integer at least \(2\), whence
\[
k\le \frac n2
\quad\text{and therefore}\quad
2nk\le n^2.
\]
Taking the maximum over eligible divisors proves \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\le n^2\).

This upper bound is attained exactly for even \(n\). Indeed, if \(n\) is even, \(k=n/2\) is a divisor and its support is
\[
\binom{2n/(n/2)}{n/(n/2)}=\binom42=6\ge4,
\]
so it is eligible and has retention \(2n(n/2)=n^2\). Conversely, equality of the maximum with \(n^2\) requires some eligible divisor \(k\) to satisfy \(2nk=n^2\), hence \(k=n/2\); integrality of this divisor forces \(n\) to be even.

Subtracting the comparator upper bound from the exact full-class value gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
&\ge 2(n-1)^2+2-n^2\\
&=n^2-4n+4=(n-2)^2>0,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the strict inequality uses \(n\ge3\). The ratio is well defined and positive: \(k=1\) is eligible because \(\binom{2n}{n}\ge\binom63=20\ge4\) for \(n\ge3\); the first inequality follows, for example, by iterating
\[
\frac{\binom{2(r+1)}{r+1}}{\binom{2r}{r}}
=\frac{(2r+2)(2r+1)}{(r+1)^2}>1
\qquad(r\ge1).
\]
Division by the positive comparator value and the bound \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\le n^2\) now give
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
\ge \frac{2(n-1)^2+2}{n^2}
=2-\frac4n+\frac4{n^2}.
\]
Because the numerator is fixed and positive, equality here is equivalent to \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=n^2\), already shown equivalent to evenness of \(n\). The displayed lower bound converges to \(2\); equality along every even \(n\) makes the ratio converge to \(2\) on that subsequence, while the universal lower bound gives limit inferior at least \(2\). Thus the full limit inferior is exactly \(2\).
